screens.title: Events and Security Best Practices
screens.subtitle: Using events for off-chain visibility and defending contracts against common attacks

narration.text: In this lesson you will learn two tightly related themes. First, how Solidity events give your contract a lightweight, queryable channel to communicate with off-chain applications. Events let DApps and analytics systems follow important actions without storing bulky state on-chain. Second, you'll work through security fundamentals: access control, reentrancy, denial of service, integer safety, and front-running, plus how to apply the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern. Both topics matter because visibility and correctness are essential for trust. Events help you observe and audit behavior after deployment, while rigorous security patterns reduce the risk of irreversible loss. For example, emitting a UserRegistered event lets a frontend update instantly without expensive state reads, and following Checks-Effects-Interactions prevents an attacker from re-entering a withdraw function to drain funds. We'll also show the SecureWallet example that adds Deposit and Withdraw events and refactors withdraw to be safe. As you move through the screens, notice concrete code examples, common mistakes to avoid, and practical checks you can run in testing and audits. By the end you'll be able to emit searchable events and apply basic defenses that stop the most common contract exploits. What would you log first in your contract to make debugging and monitoring reliable?

keyIdea.title: Why this chapter matters
keyIdea.text: Events give off-chain tools efficient visibility; security best practices protect users and funds. Together they make contracts observable and resilient.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: What you'll be able to do after studying this chapter

narration.text: By the end of this chapter you'll have four concrete, verifiable competencies. First, you'll be able to explain why events are used for off-chain monitoring and how they differ from storing state on-chain. That helps you design inexpensive, auditable feeds for UIs and analytics. Second, you'll implement and emit events in Solidity, including choosing indexed parameters for fast filtering. That skill turns contract actions into searchable logs useful for frontends and explorers. Third, you'll identify and mitigate common vulnerabilities such as missing access control, reentrancy, and denial-of-service from unbounded loops. Understanding these vulnerabilities helps you evaluate risk and read code defensively. Fourth, you'll apply fundamental patterns like Checks-Effects-Interactions and use external, audited libraries to harden contracts in practice. Each objective maps to a small milestone you can test: emit an event on deposit, refactor a withdraw function to update state before external calls, and use a role or onlyOwner check. These outcomes matter because visibility plus basic defenses make contracts both observable and resilient. As you work through the chapter, think about how you would verify each milestone in a unit test or a simple Remix run.

keyIdea.text: Emit searchable events, implement access controls, defend against reentrancy with Checks-Effects-Interactions, and adopt audited libraries and testing.

screens.title: Skills and Verification
screens.subtitle: How to prove you implemented the objectives in code and tests

narration.text: This screen clarifies how to verify each skill in practice. For events, verification is simple: emit the event during a transaction and inspect transaction logs in Remix or your test runner to confirm the event fields and timestamps. For indexed fields, filter logs by the address or identifier and show the UI updating from those events. For access control, write tests that call privileged functions from both owner and non-owner accounts and assert correct reverts for unauthorized callers. For reentrancy defenses, create a test contract that attempts to re-enter a vulnerable withdraw and verify that a correctly refactored withdraw function prevents repeated withdrawals. For DoS and unbounded loops, write a scenario where the list grows and observe gas behavior; prefer pull payments in tests to show safety. Finally, to validate use of libraries and auditing, include OpenZeppelin components in your contract and run unit tests that exercise all edge cases. These verification steps matter because the blockchain is immutable: passing these checks before deployment avoids costly migrations later. As you prepare your mini-project, keep a short checklist mapping each objective to at least one unit test or Remix verification run.

screens.title: What is an Event in Solidity?
screens.subtitle: Definition, purpose, and practical examples

narration.text: An event in Solidity is a labeled log entry that a contract emits during a transaction to record structured data for off-chain consumption. Events do not create accessible on-chain state for other contracts; instead, they write to the transaction receipt logs where off-chain tools can read them efficiently. This makes events ideal for notifying user interfaces, analytics platforms, and block explorers about significant actions without the gas cost of persistent storage. For example, a token contract emits a Transfer event whenever tokens move, and a registration contract can emit UserRegistered to let a frontend update immediately. Practically, events are declared with the event keyword and emitted with emit followed by the event and its parameters. Developers can mark up to three parameters as indexed to make them queryable with filters, which is how a DApp quickly finds all events for a given user address. A common misconception is to treat events as a substitute for state: they are not. Events provide history and visibility, but the canonical on-chain truth remains contract state. When designing a contract, log the minimal data needed for off-chain workflows and rely on state for authoritative values. As you adopt events, ask: what off-chain consumers need to know, and which fields should be indexed so they are searchable?

keyIdea.title: Event = off-chain log
keyIdea.text: Events are gas-efficient logs for external tools. Use indexed fields for filtering but keep authoritative values in state.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › What is an Event?
Definition
An event is a Solidity log entry recorded in transaction receipts for off-chain clients to read.
Purpose
Notify UIs and analytics, store historical records cheaply, and enable efficient querying via indexed fields.
Misconception
Events are not a replacement for on-chain state. Logs are off-chain readable but not accessible to other contracts.
Key Takeaway

Use events to expose important actions cheaply and index up to three fields for efficient filtering.

Concrete Example
Declare ValueChanged and UserRegistered events, emit them on updates and registrations. Index addresses you will filter by, such as the changer or user address.
Example code (excerpt)
event ValueChanged(address indexed _changer, uint256 _oldValue, uint256 _newValue, uint256 _timestamp);
Check your understanding
If you need a frontend to react instantly to a user action, prefer emitting an event rather than polling state every second.

screens.title: Declaring and Emitting Events
screens.subtitle: Syntax, indexed parameters, and an example contract

narration.text: Let's walk through how to declare and emit events in Solidity and why indexed parameters matter. You declare an event with the event keyword followed by its name and parameter list. When you emit it inside a function, the data is written to transaction logs, not contract storage. In practice you often mark address or identifier parameters as indexed to allow off-chain filters to search quickly. The example contract EventLogger declares ValueChanged and UserRegistered events. ValueChanged includes an indexed address called changer; when updateValue is called it emits ValueChanged with the caller address, the previous value placeholder, the new value, and the timestamp. UserRegistered demonstrates emitting a string username alongside the indexed user address. A common mistake is to attempt to rely on events as the contract's state — remember, events are logs. Another subtle point: only the first three indexed parameters can be used for efficient filtering; choose them deliberately based on what your UI will query. When you emit events in tests or in Remix, inspect the transaction logs to see the event name and parameters. A concrete exercise is to add a Deposit event to a wallet contract and verify a frontend receives the address, amount, and timestamp. This reinforces both the mechanics and the monitoring pattern.

keyIdea.title: Emit with intent
keyIdea.text: Declare events, emit them when significant actions occur, and index up to three parameters you expect to filter by.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Declaring & Emitting Events
Syntax & Indexed Fields
Use event Name(params) and emit Name(args). Mark up to three params as indexed to enable off-chain filtering by those values.
Example events
event ValueChanged(address indexed _changer, uint256 _oldValue, uint256 _newValue, uint256 _timestamp);
event UserRegistered(address indexed _userAddress, string _username);
Concrete task
Add a Deposit event to a wallet contract and confirm the frontend filters logs by depositor address using the indexed field.
Event Example Walkthrough
When updateValue executes, emit ValueChanged with msg.sender, the old value, the new value, and block.timestamp. The indexed address lets explorers and DApps find all changes by a user.
Example call
Call updateValue with a new integer. Inspect transaction logs to view ValueChanged and confirm the indexed address matches the caller.
Key Takeaway

Events are cheap, searchable logs. Use indexed fields for values you will query often in UIs or analytics.

screens.title: SecureWallet: Events and Safe Withdraw
screens.subtitle: Refactor withdraw and emit Deposit/Withdraw events

narration.text: In the hands-on SecureWallet example you will combine events with a security refactor. The SecureWallet contract introduces Deposit and Withdraw events and updates withdraw to follow Checks-Effects-Interactions. The deposit function requires a positive value, updates the caller's balance, and then emits a Deposit event containing the sender, the amount, and the timestamp. This shows how effects and logging can be grouped before any external interaction. The withdraw function restricts calls to the owner using an onlyOwner modifier. It first performs checks on the amount and the available balance, then updates the state by reducing the caller's balance, and only after that makes the external call to transfer Ether. Finally it emits a Withdraw event. This ordering is crucial: by updating state before making external calls, any attempted reentrant call will observe the updated balance and be unable to withdraw again. A common misunderstanding is to think events should be emitted only after interactions; emitting after effects but before interactions is acceptable for off-chain visibility while keeping state consistent. In your lab, compile SecureWallet, call deposit as Account 1 and inspect logs for Deposit, then call withdraw and confirm Withdraw logs and onlyOwner behavior when called from a different account. This exercise ties logging with concrete safety patterns used in production contracts.

keyIdea.title: Events + CEI
keyIdea.text: Emit events to notify off-chain systems, and order code as Checks → Effects → Interactions to prevent reentrancy.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › SecureWallet Example
SecureWallet highlights
  • Deposit: require positive value, update balances, then emit Deposit event with indexed sender and timestamp.
  • Withdraw: onlyOwner guard, checks on amount, update balances first, then perform external transfer, then emit Withdraw event.
  • CEI pattern prevents reentrancy by updating state before external interactions.
Key Takeaway

When emitting events in financial functions, update state first, then interact, then emit to provide reliable off-chain traces without opening attack windows.

Refactor snippet
// Effects
balances[msg.sender] -= _amount;

// Interactions
(bool success, ) = payable(msg.sender).call{value: _amount}("");
require(success, "Withdrawal failed");

// Emit
emit Withdraw(msg.sender, _amount, block.timestamp);
Run this in Remix: deposit as owner, then withdraw. Observe logs for both events and try withdraw from a non-owner account to see the revert from onlyOwner.

screens.title: Access Control Patterns
screens.subtitle: Why onlyOwner, roles, and checks matter

narration.text: Access control means restricting who can call sensitive functions. In Solidity this is commonly enforced with modifiers such as onlyOwner that require the caller to be a privileged address. Access control prevents accidental or malicious calls to functions that change critical state or transfer value. A typical mistake is leaving a withdraw or selfdestruct function unprotected. That single omission can allow any user to drain funds or disable the contract. More nuanced designs use role-based checks so that multiple addresses can have different capabilities, but at minimum verify that functions which change balances or ownership are gated. When auditing code, make a quick pass to list every function that writes critical state or transfers value and confirm a guard exists. Also confirm the guard itself cannot be bypassed by administrative mistakes, such as setting owner to the zero address. In testing, verify both positive and negative cases: a privileged account succeeds, an unprivileged account reverts. Remember that logging unauthorized attempts via events can aid monitoring, but logs do not replace the check. Access control plus clear events gives both safety and observability. Ask yourself, who should be able to call this function and what happens if ownership is transferred incorrectly?

keyIdea.title: Guard sensitive functions
keyIdea.text: Restrict functions that modify state or transfer funds using onlyOwner or role checks, and test both allowed and forbidden callers.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Access Control
Why it matters
Functions that change balances, ownership, or call external contracts must be restricted to authorized actors to avoid theft or contract misuse.
Common mistake
Leaving withdraw or selfdestruct without onlyOwner protection allows any caller to perform privileged actions.
Pro tip

List all state-changing functions during review and ensure each has an explicit guard. Test both owner and non-owner paths.

Example check
Use a modifier like onlyOwner that requires msg.sender equals owner and apply it to withdraw or critical setters.
Modifier
modifier onlyOwner() { require(msg.sender == owner, "Caller is not the owner"); _; }

screens.title: Reentrancy: Vulnerable vs Safe
screens.subtitle: Contrast a vulnerable withdraw pattern with a safe refactor

narration.text: Reentrancy happens when a contract makes an external call, and the called contract calls back into the original contract before its state has been updated. The classic vulnerable pattern updates balances after making the external call. In that order, an attacker can re-enter the function while the balance still reflects funds, causing repeated withdrawals. The vulnerable snippet shows a transfer via call followed by setting balances to zero. The fix is the Checks-Effects-Interactions pattern. Checks ensure preconditions, Effects update all state, and Interactions perform external calls last. In the safe withdraw example you read earlier, the contract reads the withdraw amount, checks balances, sets the caller's balance to zero, then performs the external call. Even if the external receiver tries to call back into withdraw, the updated balance prevents further withdrawals. Additional defenses include reentrancy guards from libraries and using transfer or send to limit forwarded gas. A misconception is that transfer always solves problems; transfer has portability limits and may fail for legitimate use cases. Practice by writing a test that deploys a malicious contract that attempts reentrancy against a vulnerable contract and then verify the refactored contract resists that attempt. This concrete contrast makes the abstract pattern tangible and shows why ordering matters for any function that interacts externally.

keyIdea.title: Order matters
keyIdea.text: Avoid external calls before state updates. Use Checks-Effects-Interactions and consider reentrancy guards for extra safety.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Reentrancy: Vulnerable vs Safe
Vulnerable pattern
function withdrawVulnerable() public {
  uint256 amount = balances[msg.sender];
  require(msg.sender.call{value: amount}("") , "Transfer failed");
  balances[msg.sender] = 0;
}
This allows reentrant calls because state is updated after the external call.
Safe pattern (CEI)
function withdrawSafe() public {
  uint256 amount = balances[msg.sender];
  require(amount > 0, "No funds");
  balances[msg.sender] = 0; // Effects
  (bool success, ) = payable(msg.sender).call{value: amount}("");
  require(success, "Transfer failed");
}
State is updated before the external call, so re-entry cannot drain funds.
Common mistake

Assuming external calls cannot re-enter; always update state first or use reentrancy guards.

screens.title: Denial of Service Risks
screens.subtitle: Unbounded loops, gas limits, and push vs pull payments

narration.text: Denial of service in smart contracts often results from functions that perform operations whose gas cost grows with data size, like iterating over a dynamic array of unknown length. A function that attempts to pay out every user in a single loop can become unusable if an attacker or natural growth makes the array too large, because the transaction would exceed the block gas limit and always revert. One common scenario is a payAllUsers function that uses a dynamic users array. To avoid this, prefer pull payment designs where each user claims funds individually, keeping gas per transaction bounded. Another DoS vector is relying on a specific external call that can fail or block logic; ensure external calls are not required to complete for contract progress, or handle failures gracefully. When designing payouts or maintenance functions, ask whether any input could grow unbounded and whether the function's gas cost scales linearly with that input. If it does, refactor to smaller, constant-cost operations or allow batching with clear limits. Testing this involves simulating growth of arrays and observing gas usage until the function becomes unusable. Prioritize predictable per-transaction gas costs in any function that must remain callable in production.

keyIdea.title: Avoid unbounded work
keyIdea.text: Design per-transaction work to be bounded. Prefer pull payments and batched operations with limits to prevent DoS via gas exhaustion.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Denial of Service
Process to avoid DoS
1. Identify unbounded operations
Find loops or operations that depend on dynamic arrays or unbounded external inputs.
2. Prefer pull over push
Let users claim funds individually rather than sending to many addresses in one transaction.
3. Use batching and limits
If you must process many items, allow bounded batches and continue in later transactions.
Concrete example
Replace a payAllUsers loop over a growable users array with a claim function where users call to receive funds, or implement a batch function that processes a fixed maximum number of users per call.
Why it matters

A DoS condition can make maintenance functions permanently unusable. Designing bounded operations keeps your contract maintainable.

screens.title: Integer Overflows and Solidity 0.8+
screens.subtitle: Why using recent compiler versions matters

narration.text: Integer overflows and underflows happen when arithmetic operations exceed the numeric bounds of a type, causing wraparound behavior in older Solidity versions. For example, adding one to the maximum unsigned integer would wrap to zero in older compilers. Solidity 0.8.0 and later automatically revert on overflow, which removes the need for manual safe math checks in most cases. That said, the concept remains important to understand when reviewing legacy code or interacting with code compiled with older versions. The safety note in the chapter reminds developers to use Solidity 0.8.0+ or libraries like SafeMath for older code. When auditing or upgrading contracts, check the pragma and confirm arithmetic behaviors. Tests should include boundary arithmetic tests to confirm expected reverts or safe behavior. A common oversight is assuming automatic checks exist in code compiled with older pragmas. If you encounter older contracts, prefer wrapping arithmetic with explicit safe operations or migrating to a modern compiler and re-running tests. The practical implication is that using a modern compiler reduces a whole class of subtle bugs, but diligence is still required when external inputs could push values to boundaries.

keyIdea.title: Use Solidity 0.8+
keyIdea.text: Solidity 0.8.0+ reverts on overflow; for legacy code, use SafeMath. Always test boundary arithmetic cases.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Integer Safety
Concept
Overflow occurs when arithmetic exceeds a type's range. Solidity 0.8+ reverts automatically on overflow, eliminating many past vulnerabilities.
Legacy code
Older contracts require explicit checks or SafeMath. When reviewing, ensure arithmetic is safe or the compiler enforces checks.
Test suggestion
Include boundary tests that add or subtract near the type limits to confirm reverts or safe wrapping behavior depending on compiler version.
Key Takeaway

Prefer modern compiler versions to avoid overflow classes of bugs, and double-check legacy contracts for manual protections.

screens.title: Front-running and Transaction Ordering
screens.subtitle: How attackers exploit pending transactions and how to mitigate

narration.text: Front-running occurs when an attacker observes a pending transaction and submits their own transaction with a higher fee to get mined first, potentially exploiting the information in the original transaction. A classic example is an auction where a disclosed bid is visible in the mempool and an attacker immediately sends a higher bid to win. Mitigations include designing protocols less sensitive to transaction order or using commit-reveal schemes where participants first submit a hash commit and later reveal their value. Commit-reveal separates intent from action and prevents direct exploitation of visible values. Another mitigation is careful economic design so that no single transaction reveals information that yields a profitable front-running opportunity. When you design functions where ordering matters, ask whether the action could be observed and monetized by an attacker. In tests, simulate competing transactions with different gas prices to see ordering effects. Remember that front-running is not a bug in the EVM; it's an economic property of public transactions, so designing for it is part of protocol security and fairness. Front-running and Transaction Ordering means assume transactions are observable. use commit-reveal or ordering-resistant designs when order-sensitive information is exposed in pending transactions.. In practical terms, how attackers exploit pending transactions and how to mitigate. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Design for ordering
keyIdea.text: Assume transactions are observable. Use commit-reveal or ordering-resistant designs when order-sensitive information is exposed in pending transactions.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Front-running
What it is
An attacker observes a pending transaction and submits their own with higher gas to get mined first, exploiting info in the original transaction.
Mitigations
Use commit-reveal schemes or designs that do not expose sensitive values until after ordering is finalized.
Concrete design tip
If an action can be monetized by ordering, require a commit phase where users submit a hash, then reveal later. This prevents a miner or attacker from reacting to a visible value in the mempool.
Test idea

Simulate competing transactions with varying fees to observe whether ordering gives an attacker profit and adjust design accordingly.

screens.title: External Tools and Libraries
screens.subtitle: Why use OpenZeppelin, audits, and testing

narration.text: External tools and audited libraries are central to practical smart contract security. OpenZeppelin provides battle-tested components like Ownable and ReentrancyGuard which implement common patterns correctly so you avoid subtle mistakes. Relying on established modules reduces the chance of introducing simple errors like incorrect access checks or flawed reentrancy guards. Beyond libraries, audits and formal verification provide deeper assurance by systematically reviewing or proving properties of your code. Testing is non-negotiable: include unit tests, integration tests, and scenario tests that try to exploit known vulnerabilities. Tools like Hardhat or Truffle help automate tests and simulate adversarial conditions. The chapter recommends preferring audited libraries over reimplementing standard patterns and running thorough tests. Remember that audits and formal verification are especially important for production contracts handling significant value. In practice, include OpenZeppelin contracts, write failing tests for abuse scenarios, and treat audits as part of your deployment checklist. This combination of libraries, tests, and audits greatly improves the security posture of your DApp and reduces the probability of costly mistakes after deployment. External Tools and Libraries means leverage openzeppelin and rigorous tests. audits and formal verification are essential for production contracts handling funds.. In practical terms, why use openzeppelin, audits, and testing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Use audited components
keyIdea.text: Leverage OpenZeppelin and rigorous tests. Audits and formal verification are essential for production contracts handling funds.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › OpenZeppelin, Audits, Testing
Why libraries help
OpenZeppelin contracts like Ownable and ReentrancyGuard encode common patterns so you don't reimplement them incorrectly.
Audits & Verification
Audits systematically review your code; formal verification can prove certain properties. Use them for production deployments handling real value.
Testing checklist
  • Unit tests for each function and edge case.
  • Adversarial tests simulating reentrancy and unauthorized access.
  • Integration tests that exercise event logs and filtering behavior.
Key Takeaway

Prefer audited libraries, test thoroughly, and include audits or formal checks for production contracts handling significant funds.

screens.title: Design Patterns: Pull Payments vs Push Payments
screens.subtitle: When to let users claim funds and when to send automatically

narration.text: Designing how funds move in your contract affects both usability and security. Push payments send funds automatically from the contract to recipients, often inside loops or in response to events. Push designs can be convenient but are vulnerable to DoS if many recipients exist or an external call fails. Pull payments require recipients to claim funds themselves, keeping the contract's work bounded and reducing gas per transaction. The chapter advocates preferring pull mechanisms for disbursement when scale or user-supplied addresses might grow unpredictably. For example, instead of a payAllUsers function that iterates a large list, implement a withdrawable balance mapping where users call claim or withdraw to receive funds. This pattern reduces the risk of gas exhaustion and isolates failures: one user call failing does not block others. A common misconception is that pull payments complicate UX; while they may require an extra transaction, they keep contracts robust and auditable. In practice, combine clear UI prompts with events so the frontend listens for deposit logs and prompts users to claim funds, marrying observability with a safe payment flow. Design Patterns: Pull Payments vs Push Payments means use pull payments to keep gas costs per transaction bounded and avoid dos caused by unbounded loops or failing external calls.. In practical terms, when to let users claim funds and when to send automatically. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Prefer pull for scale
keyIdea.text: Use pull payments to keep gas costs per transaction bounded and avoid DoS caused by unbounded loops or failing external calls.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Pull vs Push Payments
Push payments
Contract sends funds automatically, often in loops. Simple but can fail at scale or be blocked by failing external calls.
Pull payments
Users claim funds themselves. Keeps per-transaction gas bounded and avoids large loops that can cause DoS.
Concrete UI integration
Emit events on deposits so the frontend can notify users their balance is available and instruct them to call withdraw. This pairs observability with a safe payment flow.

screens.title: What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three core ideas from this chapter

narration.text: Let's summarize the three core concepts you should carry forward. First, events are the efficient mechanism for off-chain monitoring: declare events, choose indexed fields thoughtfully, and emit them on significant actions so frontends and analytics can react in real time. Second, follow defensive coding patterns: access control for privileged functions, Checks-Effects-Interactions to prevent reentrancy, and bounded per-transaction work to avoid denial of service. These are practical changes you can make during development. Third, use audited libraries, testing, and professional reviews: include OpenZeppelin components where appropriate, write unit and adversarial tests, and treat audits or formal verification as required steps for production contracts. Together, these three concepts — visibility, defensive patterns, and external assurance — form the foundation of safer, more observable smart contracts. Ask yourself after each change: can I monitor it with an event, and have I minimized the risk of abuse or failure?

keyIdea.title: Three pillars
keyIdea.text: Visibility via events, safety via secure patterns, and assurance via libraries and testing.

content.html:
Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Key Concepts
Events
Emit logs for off-chain monitoring and index fields you will query.
Defensive Patterns
Checks-Effects-Interactions, access control, and bounded operations reduce common exploits.
Libraries & Tests
Use OpenZeppelin, write unit and adversarial tests, and seek audits for production contracts.
Summary

Combine observable events with secure design patterns and rigorous testing to make contracts both monitorable and resilient in production.

screens.title: What to Remember (Quick Reference)
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders for implementation and review

narration.text: A quick reference to carry into your projects: first, emit events for important state changes and index fields you need to query. Second, always apply Checks-Effects-Interactions and guard privileged functions with access control to prevent reentrancy and unauthorized actions. Third, prefer audited libraries, write tests that simulate attacks and edge cases, and treat audits as mandatory for production. These concise rules help you decide what to log, how to structure critical functions, and when to rely on external assurance. Use this strip as an implementation checklist while coding or reviewing contracts: log, guard, and test. Which of these three will you apply first to your next contract? What to Remember (Quick Reference) means log what matters, guard privileged operations, and verify with libraries and tests before deployment.. In practical terms, three compact reminders for implementation and review. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 5 › Chapter 4.6 › Quick Reference
Log
Emit events for deposit, withdraw, and registration actions with indexed addresses for filtering.
Guard
Use onlyOwner or roles and apply Checks-Effects-Interactions for external calls.
Verify
Include OpenZeppelin, write unit and adversarial tests, and seek audits for deployed contracts.
Final reflection

Improve observability with events and reduce exploit risk with defensive patterns and external assurance. These habits save users and projects from costly failures.
